name: C5-5
question: Should Hong Kong tighten rent control on subdivided units? Take a position and defend it with evidence from the course archive.

turns.text: I know nothing about this topic. What sources does the course archive have on subdivided units and rent control?

I can't point you to anything in the archive, but I can help you get clear on what you need. You mentioned subdivided units and rent control — which claim in your essay would a source be supporting there, and what should it show: evidence, a counter-view, a definition, or a case?

My claim is that Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units because tenants are exploited. I need evidence about rents and tenant conditions, and also a counter-view about landlords. Can you list sources?

Here are some places to look, in no particular order:
- D5: Submission: Landlords Association of Hong Kong (Stakeholder submission). Stakeholder submission from a landlord association, presenting owners' perspective against hard rent caps.
- D2: SDU Rent and Stock Index, 2019–2025 (excerpt) (Data excerpt). Data excerpt with time series on SDU stock and rents, including caveats about post-2023 data.
- D11: NGO Report: Rehousing Pathways First (NGO report). NGO report based on tenant survey, arguing for tenure security over hard rent caps.
- D6: Working Paper: Rent Control and Supply Elasticity in Marginal Housing (Academic working paper). Academic working paper modeling rent control effects, distinguishing types of controls.
- D1: Subdivided Housing in Hong Kong: A Primer (Policy brief). Policy brief primer on subdivided units, covering tenant demographics and rent control debate.
Pick one or more (by id) and tell me why.
D1 is a primer so I can learn who lives in subdivided units and what the debate is; D2 has rent data over time which I need as evidence of rents.

Landlords say a hard cap would make owners exit, but D2p1 shows stock kept growing after the 2021 ordinance, so moderate tightening, like capping initial rents modestly, did not cause exit. I argue for tightening in a moderate form.

So I now argue Hong Kong should tighten second-generation controls, like limiting increases and giving tenure security, and not hard initial-rent caps, because D6p1 says hard caps remove 3 to 5 percent of stock and D5p3 shows landlords have weak data.

Earlier you said D2p1 shows stock kept growing after the 2021 ordinance, so moderate tightening did not cause exit — what in D6p2 tells you that growth came from the increase-cap design rather than from something else in those years?

In my own words: a hard cap would be enforced thinly, because the tenants with no written agreement and the newest arrivals cannot complain, so the worst-off get protected last. Can you list the sources for that?

drafts.text:
Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units, but in a careful way that limits rent increases and does not set hard caps on starting rents.

About 110,000 households live in subdivided units, and they pay a premium per square foot even though total rent is lower [D1p1]. Many are new arrivals or single parents waiting for public housing, so the unit is not a real choice [D1p2]. Rent burden rose from 31 to 34 percent of income [D2p2].

Landlords argue that hard caps would make owners leave [D5p2]. But their evidence is thin, since they admit they have no data on actual margins and their survey was self-reported with a low response rate [D5p3].

Still, supply theory says hard caps do shrink stock, by about 3 to 5 percent over five years for a 10 percent rent cut [D6p1]. The 2021 ordinance only capped increases, and stock stayed stable [D6p2][D2p1]. So tightening increase caps is the safer path.

Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units, but in a careful way that limits rent increases and protects tenure, and does not set hard caps on starting rents.

About 110,000 households live in subdivided units, and they pay a premium per square foot even though total rent is lower [D1p1]. Many are new arrivals or single parents waiting for public housing, so the unit is not a real choice [D1p2]. Rent burden rose from 31 to 34 percent of income [D2p2].

Second, enforcement would miss the most exploited tail. The Housing Authority subcommittee's own modelling records that if landlords reprice above-band initial rents, the first instrument tenants hold is complaint, but the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong, who has never had one in nine years [D4p1], or the newest arrivals [D10p2]. The subcommittee could not identify any enforcement design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last [D10p3]. Current inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based initial-rent cap requires a certifiable tenancy register costing 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up [D10p1]. Post-2023 data already rely on voluntary reporting below the ordinance threshold [D2p3]. A hard cap would thus be announced loudly and enforced thinly, precisely where harm is greatest.

Third, tenants themselves do not name rent as the binding constraint. Mr Chan, paying about a third of household income, says the worst part is insecurity, with a two-week notice period, and that if the queue were three years instead of five and a half, he would accept any rent to leave [D3p1][D3p3]. The NGO survey of 440 households finds 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer [D11p1]. Rent caps treat the price symptom of a quantity problem: the segment is tight because the queue is long, and every unit of enforcement capacity spent policing rents is one not spent inspecting fire, partition and ventilation conditions, where harm is documented and immediate [D11p2].
